title: Mahatma Gandhi and Churchill's 'Half-Naked Fakir' Jibe: The Triumph of Moral Conviction
summary: When Winston Churchill derided Mahatma Gandhi as a 'half-naked fakir' in 1931, Gandhi responded not with rancor, but with serene humor and unshakeable dignity.
full_text:
In February 1931, inside the British House of Commons, Winston Churchill delivered an impassioned speech condemning the Viceroy’s negotiations with Mahatma Gandhi:
"It is alarming and also nauseating to see Mr. Gandhi, a Middle Temple lawyer, now posing as a seditious fakir of a type well known in the East, striding half-naked up the steps of the Viceregal Palace to parley on equal terms with the representative of the King-Emperor!"

The phrase 'half-naked fakir' exploded across international newspapers. When Gandhi arrived in London later that year for the Second Round Table Conference, eager journalists surrounded him, asking whether he felt insulted by Churchill’s venomous characterization.

Gandhi smiled with unruffled serenity:
"Insulted? Not in the slightest! In fact, I am deeply indebted to Mr. Churchill for his compliment. Millions of my impoverished countrymen in India cannot afford two square meals a day, let alone fine garments. If I am to represent them truthfully, how could I wear imported wool or Savile Row suits? By describing me as half-naked, Mr. Churchill has inadvertently reminded the entire world of the stark economic reality of colonial India. He has confirmed that my clothes speak the honest truth of my people!"

By absorbing hatred with compassionate humor, Gandhi transformed an imperial insult into an enduring moral triumph.
